text: All right. Good afternoon, everybody. It is slightly after 4:30. I apologize for the delay, but at this time, I call to order the August 20, 2026, meeting of the Student Services Committee. We will begin-- I'm sorry. Let me introduce myself. My name is John Pepper of the Dulles District. I am the chair of the Student Services Committee, and joining me is school board

chair and member from the Algonquin District, Mrs. April Chandler. The third member of our committee, Ms. Carrie Labelle, is absent, but we do have quorum, so I will begin the meeting. We will start with item number two, which is public comment. In total, public comment will be limited to 10 minutes. Right now, we have one speaker for public comment, so I will give that speaker

three minutes. Before we begin, I will say thank you for engaging with the Student Services Committee and school board through the public comment process. The school board welcomes comments from Loudoun County residents and believes that strong community engagement and outreach are important components of a successful school system. Speakers must limit comments to the three minutes allotted, and all audience members shall maintain civility, decorum, and respect for the functioning and dignity of this committee at all times.
And with that, I'm going to just skip ahead and go right to public comment. And our first speaker is Victoria Rashid.

Good afternoon. I'm asking this committee not to phase out special permission. My own family does use special permission, so I understand both its value and the frustrations of the current process. That's why I believe we should fix it, not eliminate it. I keep hearing equity used to justify this change. Equity does matter. Virginia's history of segregation and white flight is very real, and Loudoun has

its own history that we should never ignore. But history is not evidence that special permission is creating inequity in Loudoun today, so show us the data. In February, LCPS reported that 2,738 special permission applications were submitted. More than one in five were from LCPS employees, and nearly two-thirds were not applications to overcapacity schools.

If you look at the total amount requested, it's 2% to 3% on average of the total student population that LCPS serves. If special permission is increasing segregation, show us. If it's harming Title I schools, show us. If it disproportionately benefits affluent families, show us. Show us which schools students are leaving, where they are going, and the demographic and socioeconomic impact.

And LCPS already collects the reasons that families request special permission, so please analyze them, because if families are disproportionately leaving particular schools, perhaps the transfer isn't the problem. Perhaps we should be asking why they want to leave. Taking away the exit does not fix what drove the family toward it. And here's the thing. This proposal creates its own equity problem. As a SEAP representative, I hear from families already struggling to navigate

special education, IEPs, 504s, and administrative processes. Now we want to add another discretionary system where parents may have to document hardship, exhaust resources, and prove their circumstances warrant an exception with no ability to appeal. I know how to navigate systems like this. I know how to find the policy, fill out the paperwork, advocate, and appeal.

Not every family does in our very diverse county. The families best equipped to navigate another layer of bureaucracy will still navigate it. How is that more equitable? And let's talk about continuity. Once LCPS approves a placement, that child builds friendships, relationships with teachers, and a community. Yet elementary families reapply every year with no guarantee that children can continue with their peers into the corresponding middle

school and then high school, the feeder system. Fix that. Approve the student through the feeder pattern subject to legitimate capacity constraints. That's time. Thank you. All right. Moving on, we will move to the approval of the June 18, 2026, draft minutes. Do I have a motion? Ms. Chandler.

Thank you, Chair Pepper. I move that we approve the draft minutes for the June 18th, 2026, committee meeting at-- Thank you. I'm going to second it, but I do have a small clerical error if we could fix that. It's the spelling of my name. It is not J-O-H-N. It is just J-O-N. So I don't know if that-- I believe because it's clerical, we do not need to approve that amendment. Okay. All those in favor of approving the draft minutes,

approving the minutes from the June 18th, 2026, meeting with the small change, say "aye." Aye. Aye. That motion passes unanimously two to zero, with Ms. Labelle absent. With that, as I've mentioned previously, we have agenda item number four, which is just a placeholder for this evening, this afternoon's presentation. But we are going to actually move ahead to item number five.

This is a discussion item, which is work time, and I specifically requested that we put this work time in place for 8155, knowing that item number six on our agenda is the action item to approve and send 8155 to the school board, and that likely will involve several amendments to the current version of 8155 that we're working

on. To help expedite the process and be able to facilitate a conversation outside of a series of amendments which may get entangled with one another, I thought that we could work through this current draft section by section with the assistance of our wonderful team from Student Services here, and therefore, do that. So I'm going to let Ms. Richardson or Mr.
Dolson, whichever one of you would like to, lead us off in our work session and I'll let you take it away.

Chair Pepper, may I ask permission for us just to go quickly through the PowerPoint presentation so we can get-- It does go over some of the amendments and some of the considerations that staff would like the committee to consider, and then we can certainly do the work session piece. Absolutely, Mr. Dolson. Okay. The floor is yours. Fantastic. Okay, so as we begin this presentation, I just wanted to give the committee the most up-to-date special permission numbers by grade level.

I'm not going to read them to you. They're up on the screen for you and are before you in your copy of the presentation. You can see that currently in Loudoun County Public Schools' 40, 26, 27 school year, we have a total of 2,811 students that are on special permission in all of our schools, and the chart here designates by grade level. The next slide shows just the work that I will say that the committee

has done over the past four years. You can see that there was a pretty sharp decline between 2025/26 and this school year, '26/27. So the goal of reducing the number of special permission applications, I do think that is definitely very clearly represented by the drastic change

from 90% to 85% threshold for school capacity. That is definitely something that my office can certainly point to when we look at the reasons for that data being shifted down. So just to our amendments that we went ahead and put in the redline policy for this evening's meeting. The amendments that we discussed at our June 2026 meeting were in line one to change the word actual to primary

We changed the section definitions to overcapacity school buildings in item A. We combined A.1 and A.1A for succinctness. We inserted a definition of school reassignment into section B, and then we also combined E1A and E1B for succinctness. And those were all amendments that were brought forward by the committee back in June.

Some of the considerations that we would like the committee to think about this evening as we go into our work session is removing the appeals process that is captured in Policy 2350 and designating an internal Loudoun County Public Schools administrative committee to hear those appeals. These decisions would be final and not appealable. Some of the options that we would like to set forward for the committee to consider are option one, having the student services director, that would be me, a level

director, so your elementary, your middle, or your high school level director, and then a level executive principal sitting on that committee. Option two would be the student services director, obviously me, a level executive principal, and then a level principal. And again, those executive principals would be based on elementary, middle, or high, and then the level principal also would be based on elementary or high.

We would also like you to consider removing the word medical from C.3B, which is the section for reasons for out-of-zone school transfers. One of the other considerations is to add rising juniors to C.3D for the reasons for out-of-zone school transfers.

Remove F.1 and move that to the 8155 regulation. We discussed this at the end of the June 2026 meeting. And then regional support information sessions to support families, we would like to have you consider that. My office would be supplying those meetings and do in-person information sessions to families.

We could certainly do it by region. We could look at where the most families that are on special permission currently attend, and we could go to those schools and answer any questions face-to-face, offering just that personable interaction with those families and try to get them to understand what the process looks like now and then what will be changing over this next school year.

We talked about 8155 in renewals, moving that to regulation, and then we discussed back in June some of the language that we might want to consider. So instead of using the term renewals, considering things like exception, prior approval, or continuation. We also suggest that placing provisions to renew special permissions for approved grade levels in Regulation 8155, and those approved grade levels and that

phase-in approach, which you'll see again that we looked over last June, will also be outlined in the regulation. And then the renewal scenarios, I will just remind you, we discussed these in detail back in June. There's scenario one, scenario two, and scenario three.

Do you have any questions regarding these scenarios and you need me to review them? Okay. Yes, please- Okay ... quickly review these scenarios for us. So in scenario one, for the '26, '27 school year, kindergarten, first, second, sixth, and ninth grade students who are currently on special permission at their school would not be able to renew. If they would like to remain at that school, they would need to use the out-of-zone

school transfer process or return to their zone schools of attendance. Students who were not approved to remain via the new out-of-zone school transfer process would then return to their zone schools of attendance. Third, fourth, seventh, tenth, and eleventh graders that are currently on special permission will be able to remain at their special permission approved school if and only if they renewed, and remember, we might use a different term

for that based on the regulation, during the appropriate window. Recall that fifth graders moving to middle school and eighth graders moving to high school are not guaranteed space availability as many of our secondary schools are already over capacity. In this scenario, each subsequent year adds an additional grade level in which renewals are no longer an option and the out-of-zone transfer becomes required to remain at a school other than their zone school of attendance.

In this scenario, the out-of-zone school transfer process becomes fully implemented by school year '30-'31. And I'll just for time's sake say that scenario two and scenario three are very similar. It's just a different approach based on the number of grade levels. If memory serves me correct, the committee was looking at scenario one and scenario three back in June as options.

And with that, that is the end of my presentation. Thank you, Mr. Dolson. I think what I would like to do, and I hope that my fellow committee member who is here would agree with me , is realistically take this policy section by section, starting with section A and going all the way through section G, I believe it is, the very end, which is relatively short.

Quickly reviewing those sections and having a very brief discussion about any changes that we wish to make. And Mr. Dolson, if you can indulge me, I know you went through a whole list of the recommendations. If there's a recommendation that fits within a section, if you could remind us as committee members what your all recommendation is, it'd be very helpful as well. So I'll start with section A, which is really the definition of overcapacity school buildings.

I don't have anything, and I know it's been changed a little bit already. I don't have anything else for section A. Ms. Chandler, do you have anything in section A at all? Okay, so we're going to leave section A as is. We're going to go relatively quickly here if both of us think that is. The next one is section B, which is on relieving overcrowding. This one, for those of you who have not gone in depth with the policy, this is

about schools that are already overcrowded and perhaps a student moves in and they need to attend a different school and the process for getting them back to where they're supposed to be. I also do not have any changes I would like to make with section B. Mrs. Chandler? I don't have any changes that I'd like to propose. I'm curious at this stage if there are any schools currently in a position

this school year who might. Could you tell me a little bit more about that? I don't have actual school names. I know there are certain schools that have no space in kindergarten. There are certain schools that have no space in second grade. They're all over the county. What I will say

is this year I have not heard as many schools as last year, but I do know that we have had some regional assignments that have already occurred. Thank you for that information. It does strike me as we can all acknowledge that there have been some demographic changes in terms of what used to happen all the time with so much population change in the county from 2000 really

until just recently. But given that we're seeing declines, I guess the only hesitancy here that I have, I acknowledge that it's still a problem and that there are certainly some schools that are impacted, is that it is a hardship for children who are moving into a community to not have access to their home school because the home school is overfull.

So that's a point well taken. If you consider some of our-- And we do have elementary schools, I would just say, that have upwards of 70 students that are currently on special permission at one elementary school. So if you subtract those 70, then you are not having to regionally assign kindergarten through fifth grade who move into that neighborhood. So that's a very good point, and that is a reality for some of our schools. There's a school in

the Sterling area, and there is a school in this Ashburn area that has a very high number of students that are on special permission. And again, it is not to say that those students aren't welcomed and loved by all of the teachers and the administrative staff at those schools. But it does create the hardship for those families that are moving in the week before school starts to find out that they are going to be attending a school other than their neighborhood school. Thank you.

Okay. So the big one for this is Section C. And Mr. Dolson, I know you had a couple that are in here as well. So we can talk about those first, or we can wait and take this in pieces. This is the largest section of the policy.

So I have a few things in here that I'd love to discuss, and the first is in the middle of Section C. The first paragraph really is the definition of out-of-zone school transfers and that parents on line 47 may not apply for an out-of-zone school transfer for students who have not yet attended their

future assigned school. I'm going to ask a question on this as well. Does this currently occur? Because I know that we have kindergartners who are applying for out-of-zone transfers, so can you explain this addition to the policy and how that changes things? So typically, this really mainly applies to rising sixth graders and rising ninth graders. Kindergartners, I will just say in my experience, parents

are applying because they have a sibling that already attends, and there could've been an attendance zone boundary change, or there could be a hardship in childcare. So typically, that's why we delay the kindergarten special permission, well, currently the special permission process, so we can really get elementary school set first, and then we start considering the kindergarten applications later on in the school year.

Regarding this specifically, we have a lot of people that are trying to apply to get to a different middle school other than their zoned school of attendance and/or a different high school other than their zoned school of attendance. And that is many of our high schools and many of our middle schools are at capacity. And so they do not have access to that school because of the capacity, number one. And number two,

we really should not be allowing students, because we're talking about students that should be going to a different middle school. And so you start to see then the differentiation between numbers of just capacity, but also how we're using our buildings and how we are-- It's also a scheduling issue when you start looking at, especially for middle school and high

schools. The resources that are being used by some schools and that are being asked to be used and they're not being used by others, that's, I think, the biggest discrepancy that this provides. Would it be beneficial, and I'm asking for your opinion on this, if after the word "parents" on line 47, we added the phrase "of middle and high school students"?

Just for clarifying purposes, since we have a little more leeway in kindergarten, and I will agree with you, that it seems that the kindergarten ones, at least I have seen, are all because they have an older sibling at that school. So I would say parents of middle and high school students. Is that amenable? Is that something that would make sense in the context of this policy?

I think the only scenarios that that might not cover- Mm-hmm ... is sometimes we have families that are just completely brand new to Loudoun. Mm-hmm And they're asking for special permission, yet they've never set foot in one of our schools. And then we also have some scenarios for home-schooled students who choose to either return to LCPS or enter public school for the

first time. And again, they also would have never set foot in our schools or their schools of residence. So while the majority that we come across, it's middle and high school, like that sixth grade, ninth grade, there are some outlying scenarios that we would want to also be thoughtful about. Would this be better served with a cutout for kindergarten, then, in another direction? Hmm.

So something along the lines of, with the exception of kindergarten siblings, parents may not apply. I'm trying to think of a way. I like policies that are a little more black and white. Ms. Chandler? No. Okay. So my wonder would be if there could be something in the policy regarding parents

of kindergartners to be directed to the regulation. The only reason I say that is because we can't predict the number of kindergartners that are going to be enrolling in any school. And then we obviously can't predict the number of parents of kindergartners who are going to then possibly want to apply for an out-of-zone school transfer. We could create language that would allow us some

leeway and explain how the process works to include reasons why kindergarten parents can apply for an out-of-zone school transfer that's going to mirror very similarly to the reasons why any parent should be applying for out-of-zone school transfers. I do agree with what Ms. Richardson said. What we tend to see in some cases that would be the outlier

is parents that are moving from out of state that move into Loudoun and they want their kid to go to said school, and they've really had no experience in Loudoun County whatsoever. Okay. Ms. Chandler. So I'd love it if we could start with having you reflect on your proposal again. Could I hear your proposal again? So my initial proposal was- From the beginning? Sure ... on line 47. Mm-hmm. After the word "parents," add the phrase "of middle and high school students." So

the line 47 would now read, "Parents of middle and high school students may not apply for an out-of-zone school transfer for students who have not yet attended their future assigned school." Oh, okay, so you're in the clean copy. I'm in the clean copy. I'm sorry. That's okay. It was easier for me with the clean copy on this one. Okay. I would express some hesitancy about creating different rules- Mm-hmm ... for different levels. I don't know.

I feel like it might be helpful for me to understand the types of scenarios, and I say that as someone who sat on the appeals committee now for three sessions. We've done it three years. At high school, for example, you might see someone apply for special permission because they want to play on a particular team with a particular coach.

There might be a perception about the type of community or the neighborhood. Could you speak to some of the other just general types of reasons that we see why people in high school are applying for special permission? So I think the most typical we get is that the student has attended the feeder middle school, and they want to remain with their friends.

Okay. So that's an interesting point, because what is missing and what I'm trying to consider is what would motivate someone to choose a particular middle school. High school, you could see tracking towards college applications, a perception that some are going to give you a better position. But with middle school, really what you're seeing is that students have maybe started in a feeder school that goes into that, and so it is

families trying to stay within the feeder. That is the most typical application that we get, yes. We should not be getting parents asking to be on a specific team, because that really comes into BHSO violations. So that would be something we would not consider at all. I'm sorry, go ahead.

They may enter into the special permission system at a different level with that intent, though. Yes, that's correct. To be perfectly fair, in our community, people start playing on certain teams because they want to play ball in high school when they're in elementary school. That's just part of being in Loudoun. That's true. That's very true. Yes. Okay. So what we're seeing really is that families get accustomed to being in a

place and want to stay in a place, regardless of whether or not their house is connected to that place. Yes, I would say that is the most typical application that we get, and reason for requesting special permission, yes. Okay. Okay. So maybe I'll ask you all this, piggybacking off what we were just talking about. Is there a sentence we could add that could direct parents to a regulation that we could put about kindergarten?

So when I read this, I think our conversation is that we need to keep the sentence as is, but there needs to be some sort of caveat for kindergarten students. And like you said, I believe the vast majority of them are students with siblings already in the school. Do you have a suggestion for us?

Something along the lines of parenthetical See Regulation 8155? I think it- Yeah. Okay. I feel like that would be the easiest and most transparent way, and then we would just create something very specific in the regulation for parents of kindergartners. Perfect. I think that's the way to go. So we can add a parenthetical

after, I guess it would be at the end, in the middle of line 49 on the non-red line version, or it'd be on line 63 of the red line version. Okay. Appreciate that. So the other piece I want to talk about is what we were just discussing.

One of the things that I would love to see, I would love your opinion on why this is becoming such an issue is when we apply for out-of-zone school transfers, and this backs onto reason three, there's a whole list of reasons. I'm a big believer in continuity. I think continuity is best for our children K-12,

and I would like to see a situation in place where once a student is accepted into a school within a pyramid, that they're able to continue within that pyramid. I know that there's some weird factors in there. We have a lot of split-feed elementaries, and capacity levels change. But on lines

54 through 59, it talks about the non-continuation and the reapplication for special permissions. I really struggle with that because as someone who's sat in the appeal hearings, that's a lot of the appeals that we see, is students who want to continue high school with their peer groups that they made in middle school. Particularly, those students who had a difficult time at whatever school they were starting at, and for social or emotional reasons, went to a new middle school, had

a great experience, and then wish to continue. I think I'd just love to hear people's thoughts on that. So Chandler, do you have anything you'd like to add on that? I have a lot of thoughts. I think we all do. This has been a journey, and I will say, as a candidate, I struggled with the whole idea of this, and it's really just based on what I

witnessed as a parent in the particular feeder where I live, right? Having sat through three years of appeals, I do feel that I saw some scenarios where it felt fair and appropriate to make some assignments. But when I reflect on those scenarios, I think the policy

captures a lot, maybe all, of the times where that would be most appropriate. We've talked a great deal about this policy as a school board, and in particular to this committee, and there have been some things that have been revealed throughout that process that I don't think that the wider community understands. So even though we may have talked about it before, I would like to review some key

components. How did this policy come to exist? Thank you for your question, Mrs. Chandler. The policy was initially created in 1970. The basis of this policy was segregation. Loudoun County was integrating by law. We had sections of the county that did not fully integrate

until about 1976, and so the basis, the foundation for this policy was for there to be the choice for families not to go with other families to school that they did not feel comfortable with. And so now this policy has been in place since 1970? Since 1970. 56 years? Yes. And it's 2026. Yes.

And in Loudoun County, we serve one of the most diverse student populations in the country. Yes, we do. And so in looking at the numbers, one of the first calculations that I made, you pulled up our new dashboards, which I'm so excited about, and confirmed that as of right now, understanding that the data lags by about a day, there's currently

77,514 students. And then given the current LCPS special permissions that were approved for '26, '27, with a total number of 2,811 students, that's 3.6% of our student population that's participating in special permission. Could you categorize for us how much time and effort your department spends

on this process for 3.6% of the population? I would say it's probably 80% to 85% of a team of three of us. Well, for my part, the team of two, it's 100% of what they do. So team of two, 100% of what they do. My part is probably about 85%.

Okay. And so in my journey as a school board member, when I was doing all the school visits, especially in my own community, one of the questions that I asked was, what makes parents make this choice? And repeatedly, I heard that it's a choice of privilege, that parents who have the capacity, time, space to build in the opportunity

to drive their children to school, who don't depend on transportation, may be shopping for schools that are perceived to be better Than others in the 100 schools that we serve here in LCPS. And we've had, throughout this process, principals who've come and who've shared

with us some of the problems that happen when you're a school that's perceived to be less than. Could we review that? Absolutely. I can speak from experience in having served in a school that felt less than as a principal. Losing students, losing families to this policy, not a good feeling. We had, I believe, Mr. Frew, who was here from Sterling Middle School. He shared.

Dr. Brewer, last year, the last committee, he came to speak to this. Dr. Hitchman, who was receiving a lot of people. I believe Mr. Blubaugh from Algonkian Elementary School early on in the process spoke as well. And I think more so than, so I'm going to speak from the school-based administrative side. It is also the

difficulty in planning for these families, these students, when you get your numbers, and again, we try to go through all the applications as quickly as we can, but that process does take time, and we have to then provide appeals, and we have to then provide, in some cases, additional staffing at the last minute, because we have gone over a

classroom size, or we've gone over the special education capacity for that school building. So it's additional. Even though the policy says we, meaning myself and Ms. Richardson and Ms. Carpenter, cannot do that. If the school board chooses, we have to then figure out a way to make sure that the students' needs are met. So what I will say is having prepared for students, you get your number, and then you also then get the number of

students that are leaving your school building. Having to look at a teacher who started her first or second week of school and say, "You're being transferred to another school because my student enrollment has dipped to 150," and I get a call from human resources saying we have to transfer her because there's a higher need. That's a difficult conversation to have as well. It's also difficult for that receiving principal to then build a schedule that

meets the students' needs. So there are a lot of moving parts to this that, again, and I think you said it very well, Ms. Chandler, aren't necessarily out there for the public's eye. We just make it happen because that's what we do. We're here to serve kids. But I do think we, if memory serves me correct, we have provided the committee a lot of perspectives from the school-based perspective in what this

policy, and I'm not saying this policy has malintent all over it. I do think it just does create a lot of difficulties. And we have good schools in Loudoun County. That's all I'm going to say. We have great schools in Loudoun County. Okay. So the next question that I have is, are we aware of any other school

divisions in the region or in the Commonwealth that have a similar practice that still exists today? Yes. We have neighboring counties, Fairfax, Prince William. I'm just going to name Arlington, I believe. Do they have special permission as it exists today? Not in the same spirit as we. It is more of a transfer process where they can apply to transfer

schools for specific reasons, very similar to what we have outlined in our out-of-zone school transfer process. Not necessarily for, I just want to go to this school because I want to go to this school. Thank you. That's what I was getting at. So what we're doing in creating this policy change is bringing Loudoun County into alignment with what the evidence-based best practices are that are existing across the region and across the Commonwealth, and that there will still be

opportunities for families to apply, but the situations are appropriate, and the decisions will be made by experts who are educators with a professional background that have the best capability to make the decision, as opposed to elected school board members, on whether or not that process and that request is appropriate. And so there will

still be the ability to change schools, but it's based on situations, mental health, whether or not there's a work-related component. Maybe we could talk a little bit about those. So specifically, the reasons that we were talking about. So we have childcare. That is

something that we would reserve for elementary. The emotional or social adjustment reason. Within that would be the ability for, or the requirement, I should say, for parents to complete a form that shows, and I say that hardship, it showed that need. We have, obviously, an employee who is working for the school system as a perk. Again,

as a consideration, we have added the idea of including juniors and seniors into this. A majority of the applications that we saw, or the renewals, and I will say some of the hardships that we had this year were because of the attendance boundary changes that occurred. Juniors were not included in some of that.

And that, as a former high school English teacher, I love teaching 11th grade, that was something that really opened my eyes to that. So we are bringing that forward as a consideration. And then obviously the family relocation and the family move in, and the family relocation moving out. So those are our reasons. We would also then, just going back to the first reason for childcare, we would research that.

And I will say previously, that has been something that prior to me coming in this role, I would say maybe 10 to 15 years ago, when it was really only an office of one person, and it was actually the person, Ms. Richardson's administrative assistant, who was doing all this. She was doing the research for who was receiving the childcare, where was it, what was the closest elementary school.

So we would like to resurrect that process so we are sure that the person who is truly getting childcare is asking for the right school. Thank you. And truly thank you for your patience with me as we've gone through this. I like to sort of lay the setting, right? And I think it's important that we capture this on the record for the community to

understand because it is a big change. And the more clear we are about the reasons why, I think it's easier to understand. That said, in the past, I have also reflected on the fact that this system has existed, and I do want us to take a cautious approach to how we unravel it. Okay.

So I'm going to first of all, Ms. Chandler, thank you so much for your comments. I actually believe at the core level, almost identical to what you just stated. And I also want to thank Ms. Richardson, Ms. Dolson, your entire team, for these six reasons as to why someone should request an out-of-zone school transfer. What it's doing is it appears to be eliminating just the willy-nilly idea of choice. I just want to leave because of choice.

That being said, I think because of this, it kind of goes back to my initial question. The vast majority of what we're going to see based on this policy, you're going to have your move-ins and your move-outs and your rising juniors and seniors, which will actually wash away if we look at the charts that you were, the step-down charts. The vast majority of what we're going to see for out-of-zone school transfer is going to be because of reason B and possibly reason C.

Reason C is the employee perk. I don't ever want to touch that.
